narrative:
The model predicts you have a 37% chance of failing your final year. This isn't a certainty, but it's high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to help strengthen your performance before it's too late.

The prediction is driven mainly by three key aspects of your situation. By far the strongest factor is that you have already failed one class in the past. Among students who passed, almost none had any previous failures, so this history strongly pushes the model toward expecting you to fail again. 

Two other factors pulled in the opposite direction, working to support a passing outcome. First, your family has three or fewer members, which is less common than larger families among students who succeeded. Second, you have a clear desire to pursue higher education, something every student who passed also shared. These elements helped reduce the predicted risk, but unfortunately they were not strong enough to overcome the impact of your past academic setback.

To improve, focus on addressing the pattern of past failure. Since you want to continue studying after school and have family support at home, consider creating a more consistent daily study routine beyond the current less-than-two-hours per week. Talk to your teachers about targeted help in the subjects that have challenged you before. Small, steady changes now can still shift your final result.
